::: {.why}
Every ratio in the next two weeks divides by something, and choosing what you subtract first is a modelling decision that most published numbers make silently.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Say what a long-short market-neutral book earns on its cash, and what the correct risk-free adjustment for it is.
- Show, with your own numbers, how much of a reported Sharpe ratio can come from the choice of risk-free rate alone.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Finish the comparison you started last night: SPY Sharpe with and without the bill rate, in two eras. Report four numbers and the difference in each era. The 2004-2007 gap is the one that should change how you read any Sharpe published before 2009.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Work out the cash mechanics for three books on paper: fully invested long-only, 100 long and 100 short, and a futures position with 5 percent margin posted. For each, say what balance earns interest, what balance pays it, and what the correct excess-return definition is.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Add `excess_returns(returns, rf)` to qlib/returns.py, taking an annualised rate series and converting it to the daily convention correctly. Getting the day-count conversion right here saves an argument with yourself in week 43.
:::
:::
